title: Tadhg's scorched stone
summary: At the black well two valleys east, Tadhg holds up a dark-faced stone before a gathering and swears the lightning struck his own family's well, not the mason's. The mason's household hears of it and answers nothing, keeping the fire rather than the argument.

title: The young well's telling
summary: An old woman of the young well to the south begins to tell, softly and without a stone to prove it, that her own mother saw the lightning fall into their well and not the mason's. The telling travels further than Tadhg's louder claim and outlasts it.

title: Three tellings held at once
summary: The high valleys settle, without any household deciding it outright, into three tellings of where the lightning fell, held side by side and never set against each other. Only the scorched lip of the mason's own shaft still shows the truth of it, plainly, to anyone who walks to see.

title: Muirne born
summary: A daughter is born at Tobar dhìreach, a great-granddaughter of Conall's line, and is given young to the household's hearth-keeper to be raised among the fire before she is raised among words. She is named Muirne.

title: Muirne takes up the watch of the well-cut
summary: Not yet grown, Muirne begins to keep the winter watch over the burning vein as the keeper before her tires of the work, sitting the dark half of the year on the two flat stones as every keeper has sat since Conall.

title: Muirne marks the vein-fire sinking
summary: Keeping a private reckoning against her own memory, Muirne comes to see what no keeper before her has said aloud: that the glow in the well-cut grows a little lower with every winter, the vein burning down like any fire that is fed by nothing but itself.

title: The vein-fire burns low
summary: Through the years of Muirne's watch the glow in the broken vein fades winter on winter, unmarked by most of the valley, whose hundred hearths no longer need it, and marked only by the one keeper who sits with it in the cold.

title: The last ember
summary: In a wet spring of failed crops and standing water, Muirne sits out the last night of the vein-fire in the rain and watches its pale glow go out, quietly, with no one else there to see the mason's fire die in the ground where it was struck.

title: Muirne refuses the digging
summary: When talk turns to deepening the well-cut in hope of striking fire again, Muirne stands at the mouth of it and forbids the digging, saying the fire came out of the sky on one night only and is not a thing to be dug after in the ground.

title: The slab laid over the vein
summary: The household levers a broad flat stone across the mouth of the mason's well-cut and packs its edge with turf, sealing the burnt vein from the weather and forbidding any water to be drawn near it again.

title: The new well cut
summary: A stone's throw from the covered vein, the household cuts a fresh well that gives clean water from its first day, and it is this well, not the mason's old cut, that the household draws from from that day on.

title: Muirne dies
summary: Muirne dies at Tobar dhìreach in old age and is buried in the ground near the house with no coal or fire laid beside her, having already given the vein's fire, whole, back to the stone. The telling of the slab passes to her grandchildren.
